skyline.text: Why Amit Varma stood up for a pod­caster no­body would de­fend
Ajay Shah on why an in­firm state calls for fewer curbs
Why every right flows from a new­born own­ing it­self

masthead.footnote: *The right to free speech is absolute. Page 2

brief.head: Over to the bench
brief.text: People who want black-and-white laws on in­cite­ment, Ajay Shah said, are not re­spect­ing the com­mon law, where judges read sub­tle cases and draw the line. {088-C08}

brief.head: Blocked, not banned
brief.text: Blocking some­one on Twitter is not cen­sor­ship, Amit Varma said: no one is en­ti­tled to your at­ten­tion. The bat­tle for free speech is against the state. {088-C09}

brief.head: Rumour control
brief.text: The gov­ern­ment has forced com­pa­nies to watch so­cial media and rebut ru­mours about them. That is “just dumb”, Ajay Shah said: a firm should be busy doing its busi­ness. {088-J18}

brief.head: Snowflake nation
brief.text: Why watch a show you dis­like? Get a life, Ajay Shah said. India has a snowflakes prob­lem, he ar­gued: peo­ple so in­se­cure that mere words wound them. {#snowflakes}

brief.head: Mature enough
brief.text: To those who say Indians are too sen­si­tive for free speech, Amit Varma replied that India has ne­go­ti­ated greater di­ver­sity than any other part of the world, for cen­turies. {#meltingpot}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.who: Amit Varma, on what a case under Section 295A costs the accused, whatever the verdict

lead.kicker: Amit Varma makes the case for free speech absolutism
lead.head: No shades of grey on speech

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 88

play.label: Hear the case in six clips

body: Amit Varma says he is all shades of grey on facts, be­cause the world is too com­pli­cated to un­der­stand in its en­tirety. On cer­tain val­ues he is black and white, and free speech is one of them. {088-C01}
“I am a free speech ab­so­lutist[[x1]],” he said, and with Ajay Shah he set out what that means and how it has fared in India.
## What set it off

The episode was top­i­cal, a rar­ity for a show that aims to be time­less. The pod­caster Ranveer Allahbadia had asked a crude ques­tion about par­ents and in­cest on *India’s Got Latent*, a sub­scrip­tion-only com­edy show on YouTube.

A clip went viral, the right piled on, and then the state stepped in: po­lice cases, a pass­port taken away, an order to pro­duce no more con­tent. Around forty peo­ple con­nected to the show faced cases, in­clud­ing the ed­i­tor.
Varma, who has never watched a full episode of Allahbadia’s show, tweeted that he was a well-intentioned kid who had apol­o­gised grace­fully. Left and right both came down on Varma.
“A fun­da­men­tal prin­ci­ple of free speech is you should de­fend the peo­ple that you dis­agree with the most,” he said. {088-S02}
His fear is that a hated tar­get lets the state bring in a broad­cast bill through the back door, or sim­ply nor­malise treat­ing cre­ators this way.
## Three ar­gu­ments

Varma’s first ar­gu­ment comes from first prin­ci­ples. Following John Locke, a new­born child owns it­self, not the king or the state, and every right flows from that. Silence some­one and you deny their per­son­hood and agency.
The sec­ond is the mar­ket­place of ideas, where ideas com­pete and, in Matt Ridley’s phrase, have sex. An of­fi­cial view can be wrong, and progress, Varma said, comes from heretics.
The third is democ­racy, a con­test of ideas about how to run a coun­try. Punish one person’s speech and oth­ers think twice: elec­toral ma­nip­u­la­tion with­out touch­ing a bal­lot box.
## A constable’s Constitution

India, Varma ar­gued, never en­shrined free speech at all. Article 19(1)(a) grants it; Article 19(2) at once al­lows “rea­son­able re­stric­tions” on vague grounds such as pub­lic order, de­cency and moral­ity.

Who in­ter­prets them? The po­lice con­sta­ble, he said, re­call­ing Somnath Lahiri’s protest in the con­stituent as­sem­bly that fun­da­men­tal rights had been framed from a constable’s point of view. {088-C04}
That is why colo­nial-era laws such as 295A, 153A and the sedi­tion law, 124A, sur­vive in India, though they no longer exist in Britain.

When sedi­tion was struck down in the early 1950s, Jawaharlal Nehru an­swered with the First Amendment. {088-S04} Syama Prasad Mookerjee asked him what prece­dent he was lay­ing down if “some other party comes into au­thor­ity”.

The elites, Varma said, fail in two ways. They in­fan­tilise cit­i­zens, and they are hyp­ocrites, con­demn­ing speech laws used against their side and cheer­ing when those laws hit their en­e­mies. {088-C06}
To the stan­dard ob­jec­tions he had an­swers. Falsely shout­ing fire in a crowded the­atre is al­ready tres­pass and harm; if hate speech leads to vi­o­lence, pun­ish the vi­o­lence.
His line is America’s: all speech, hate speech in­cluded, short of di­rect in­cite­ment to vi­o­lence. “Here is Ajay Shah’s ad­dress, go and lynch him” is where it is crossed.

Shah, clos­ing, pushed the case fur­ther. Because fil­ing a case in India is it­self the pun­ish­ment, he ar­gued, the coun­try needs “even lower re­stric­tions on free speech” than coun­tries such as the UK, not the same.

second.label: Art and provocation
second.head: Verses yes, cartoons no?
second.deck: Amit Varma rejects an MP’s line between a novel and a cartoon

pic.caption: Salman Rushdie at the Berlin launch of his book “Knife” in 2024

body: Around 2007 or 2008, dur­ing the vi­o­lence over the Danish car­toons, a man Amit Varma calls per­haps the most sen­si­ble MP in the coun­try today wrote a col­umn. Varma would not name him. {088-S07}
The MP said he sup­ported Salman Rushdie and *The Satanic Verses*, but not the Danish car­toon­ists. {#rushdie} The novel, he ar­gued, was a work of art; the car­toons were mere provo­ca­tion.

Varma re­jects the dis­tinc­tion. You might like the novel and find the car­toons ob­nox­ious and re­pul­sive, he said, but both have an equal right to free speech. Such hypocrisy, he added, is ram­pant around us today.

quote.text: They’re ab­so­lutely equal. If you’re going by prin­ci­ple, you have to sup­port both.

third.head: Moved by the moving image

pic.caption: Amit Varma on books, films and the censor

body: In 1968 K.A. Abbas made *A Tale of Four Cities*, a doc­u­men­tary set in Mumbai’s red-light dis­tricts. It was ob­jected to, and the mat­ter went all the way to the Supreme Court.

The court ruled that cin­ema needed closer scru­tiny than the writ­ten word. Amit Varma read from the judg­ment: “a per­son read­ing a book or other writ­ing or hear­ing a speech or view­ing a paint­ing or sculp­ture is not so deeply stirred as by see­ing a mo­tion pic­ture.” {088-S05}
That rea­son­ing, Varma said, is why film cen­sor­ship ex­ists: a board of bu­reau­crats de­cides what is fit for Indian so­ci­ety, be­cause peo­ple are thought so im­pres­sion­able. {#board}
“We have nor­malised it, we take it for granted,” he said, call­ing it “such a deeply ob­jec­tion­able way of think­ing”.

box.title: The book behind the history
box.text: Tripurdaman Singh’s *Sixteen Stormy Days* tells the story of the First Amendment, the episode that hob­bled free speech in India’s Constitution. Amit Varma calls it bril­liant and says ev­ery­one should read it. Singh also dis­cussed it on Varma’s pod­cast. {088-R01}

sections.label: Three arguments
sections.head: Let a hundred heretics bloom
sections.caption: the three arguments for free speech
body: Amit Varma has been writ­ing col­umns on free speech for more than twenty years. {#columns} He laid out the three big ar­gu­ments he has made through all of them.
The first is from first prin­ci­ples, and runs through John Locke[[x2]]. When a new­born child is born, who owns it? Not so­ci­ety, not the state, not a king. A child owns it­self[[x3]]. {#locke}

From that right to self-ownership flow the oth­ers: to life, to prop­erty, and to free ex­pres­sion, be­cause your thoughts are your own. To si­lence some­one, Varma said, is to deny their per­son­hood and agency, and an at­tack on one person’s agency is an at­tack on everybody’s.
## Ideas in the mar­ket­place

The next two ar­gu­ments come from con­se­quences. In a free mar­ket­place of ideas, ideas com­pete and re­com­bine, or, in Matt Ridley’s phrase, ideas have sex, and the best ones come to the fore. {088-R08}
If the state pre­scribes one view of the world, that view may be wrong. You should be free to say the earth goes around the sun, Varma said, and equally free to say the op­po­site. {088-C03}

~ The third ar­gu­ment is democ­racy, which Varma de­fined as a com­pe­ti­tion be­tween dif­fer­ent points of view about the best way to run a coun­try. Punish one person’s speech, he said, and to­mor­row oth­ers will think twice be­fore say­ing the same thing. That chill­ing ef­fect is elec­toral ma­nip­u­la­tion with­out a rigged booth. {#chilling}

quote.text: Progress comes from heretics. Progress comes from peo­ple say­ing that the earth goes around the sun and not vice versa

sections.label: The history
sections.head: Constitution, now a periodical
sections.caption: India’s troubled history of free speech
body: For Amit Varma, the gold stan­dard of free speech is the US First Amendment: “Congress shall make no law” abridg­ing the free­dom of speech or of the press. No caveats, no ex­cep­tions. {#gold}

India’s Constitution is an­other mat­ter. Drawing on Subhashish Bhadra’s *Caged Tiger*, Varma said con­sti­tu­tions are prod­ucts of their cir­cum­stances. {088-R05} India’s was framed amid tur­moil, with more than five hun­dred princely states, so it cen­tralised power[[x5]] and paid lip ser­vice to free­dom.
India, Varma said, ex­changed white-skinned rulers for brown-skinned ones: the colo­nial state, built to rule sub­jects[[x4]] rather than serve cit­i­zens, was adopted whole­sale.
## Lacking a the­ory of the state

Ajay Shah would not fault the in­di­vid­u­als in the con­stituent as­sem­bly, who rep­re­sented the in­tel­lec­tual cap­i­tal of India. “But I think that they were just lack­ing in their un­der­stand­ing of the state,” he said. {#theory}

Leaders from Nehru and Indira on­wards amended the Constitution so often to do un­con­sti­tu­tional things, Varma said, that a car­toon of the time had a par­lia­ment book­store clerk ex­plain that he did not stock pe­ri­od­i­cals. {088-J09}
~ Varma re­called that in the early 1950s even Ambedkar, once proud of the Constitution, said he would gladly burn it him­self. {088-J17}

quote.text: I feel that many of these fun­da­men­tal rights have been framed from the point of view of a po­lice con­sta­ble.
quote.who: Somnath Lahiri, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The elites
sections.head: The masses are not the problem
sections.caption: infantilisation and hypocrisy
body: Power cor­rupts char­ac­ter, Amit Varma said, and not just in the ob­vi­ous sense of want­ing more money. The found­ing gen­er­a­tion were the best and bright­est, but prox­im­ity to power bred ar­ro­gance. {088-C05}
He named two fail­ings of the elites. The first is in­fan­til­i­sa­tion: treat­ing cit­i­zens as in­ca­pable of de­cid­ing for them­selves. Film cen­sor­ship came out of ex­actly that think­ing.

Varma was re­cently on a pod­cast co-hosted by a for­mer guest of *The Seen and the Unseen* who is close to the Congress party. She said we need to up­lift the con­scious­ness of the masses. Varma’s reply: “No, masses are not the prob­lem, you are the prob­lem.” {088-S08}
## Laws for thee

The sec­ond fail­ing is hypocrisy. A prom­i­nent fig­ure on the left told Varma that 295A and 153A were bad laws, then in the same breath sug­gested to a col­league fil­ing a 295A case against a right-wing politi­cian.
“If you agree it is bad, it is bad, pe­riod,” Varma said. “You can’t say that don’t use it against us, but I will use it against the enemy.” {088-S06}

~ His ad­vice for any free speech con­tro­versy: don’t per­son­alise it, don’t politi­cise it. Who de­cides what is of­fen­sive? Today it may be your friend, to­mor­row your enemy, he said, and the best way past that is to be an ab­so­lutist. {088-C02}

quote.text: Many peo­ple who claim to be for free speech are ac­tu­ally for free speech they agree with.

art.caption: Amit Varma on infantilisation and hypocrisy

sections.label: The objections
sections.head: Punish the act, not the word
sections.caption: the standard objections
body: Ajay Shah asked Amit Varma to take on the canon­i­cal cases where speech is said to cause harm. Varma began with the cliché of falsely shout­ing fire in a crowded the­atre, a line from Oliver Wendell Holmes in 1919 in a judg­ment later over­turned. {#holmes}
The law should pun­ish it, Varma said, but it has noth­ing to do with free speech. The shouter tres­passes on the owner’s prop­erty, and causes or at­tempts harm to oth­ers.
Hurt feel­ings he dis­missed: they are sub­jec­tive and could cover any­thing. “We are adults,” he said, not kinder­garten chil­dren ask­ing teacher to take away someone’s tif­fin box. {088-J11}
## Where the line falls
If hate speech leads to vi­o­lence, pun­ish the vi­o­lence, and the speaker too as an ac­ces­sory, but only if there was di­rect in­cite­ment[[x6]]. {088-C07}

Shah tested the line with a tweet or­der­ing Varma’s 100,000 fol­low­ers to dunk a glass of cold water on the head of Nomsita, who edits the show. Being wise and sen­si­ble, they would know it was hu­mour. Telling the two apart, Shah said, is what com­mon-law judges are for. {088-J07}
~ Libel be­longs in civil courts, Varma said, and fraud is fraud, not speech. Shah’s ex­am­ple: a medicine that claims 100mg of sal­i­cylic acid and con­tains 50mg. {#fraud}

quote.text: If some­one com­mits vi­o­lence be­cause of some­thing I say, you catch that per­son and you pun­ish the vi­o­lence

art.caption: Amit Varma on the standard objections

sections.label: Ajay’s word
sections.head: Weak state, strong speech
sections.caption: why India needs freer speech
body: Ajay Shah added a layer the usual de­bates leave out: state ca­pa­bil­ity[[x7]]. What works in Germany or the UK can­not be me­chan­i­cally trans­planted to India.

Filing a crim­i­nal or civil case and going through the courts is it­self the pun­ish­ment, he said, and po­lice, pros­e­cu­tors and judges do not work well. So India needs even lower re­stric­tions on free speech than the West, not the same. {088-C10}
That should hold, Shah said, for the next hun­dred years, while India is still fig­ur­ing out the ba­sics of how to be a democ­racy.
## A mar­ket in opin­ions
Truth, Shah ar­gued, is too high a bar for speech. Most of the world is a fog of war, and if you could speak only with doc­u­men­tary proof, you would hardly speak at all.

Securities and de­riv­a­tives mar­kets are pure mar­ket­places of opin­ion. A short seller who bets against a com­pany and then pub­lishes dam­ag­ing claims puts his money where his mouth is, and de­serves more re­spect than a ran­dom YouTuber diss­ing Infosys. {088-C11}

~ Finally, cred­it­ing their friend Suyash Rai, Shah said every medium of pro­pa­ganda, from Mussolini’s radio to LLMs, has a learn­ing curve. People once be­lieved ev­ery­thing on WhatsApp; today no­body does. Let these things play out, he said, rather than use state power. {088-C12}

quote.text: You need even lower re­stric­tions on free speech in India be­cause of the in­fir­mi­ties of the state.
Whether or not we like the peo­ple in power at one par­tic­u­lar point in time. The only way to safe­guard a democ­racy is through free speech.

p3.title: Tales from the dock
p3.deck: Four tales of words, power and the people caught between them

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why he defended a podcaster he does not watch
stories.head: Stand by the man you can’t stand
body: Ranveer Allahbadia, the pod­caster known as BeerBiceps, runs a madly pop­u­lar show. Amit Varma has never watched a full episode, but sees him as a sin­cere young man, cu­ri­ous and no kind of winger, left or right.

Then he went on *India’s Got Latent*, a sub­scrip­tion-only YouTube show started by the edgy co­me­dian Samay, and asked a crude ques­tion about in­cest and par­ents. It was not even orig­i­nal, Varma said: an old Reddit ques­tion, used by a much big­ger co­me­dian seven years be­fore.

A sub­scriber put a clip on­line. It went madly viral, the right wing jumped on it, and then the state got in­volved: po­lice cases in sev­eral places in­clud­ing Assam, a pass­port taken away, an order to pro­duce no more con­tent.

Around forty peo­ple con­nected with the show faced cases, in­clud­ing the ed­i­tor. An ed­i­tor cuts things out, Varma noted, but cut ev­ery­thing ob­jec­tion­able from a com­edy show and noth­ing is left. {088-J05}

Varma jumped into the fray. He tweeted that Allahbadia was a well-intentioned kid who had apol­o­gised grace­fully, and that any­one who did not like the show should not watch it. {088-S02} Both left and right came down on him equally hard.

He was de­fend­ing not the joke, nor even the man, he said, but the right. And Hanlon’s razor ap­plied: never at­tribute to mal­ice what can be ad­e­quately ex­plained by stu­pid­ity, or here per­haps ig­no­rance. {088-J15}
~ Nobody has rea­son to de­fend Allahbadia, which is the dan­ger. A hated tar­get lets the state slip a broad­cast bill through the back door, or nor­malise treat­ing cre­ators this way.
stories.why: When ev­ery­body is beat­ing up a guy, Varma said, that is the time to speak for him. Free speech is tested by the peo­ple no­body wants to de­fend, since tools nor­malised against them can later reach any­one.
stories.postscript: Varma some­times jok­ingly calls him Tequila Triceps, after the fit­ness chan­nel Allahbadia first tried.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Ranveer Allahbadia affair

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Nehru and the First Amendment
stories.head: Amend first, ask questions later
body: In the early 1950s, Jawaharlal Nehru was crack­ing down on speech, from the RSS mag­a­zine *The Organiser* to Romesh Thapar’s com­mu­nist mag­a­zine *Crossroads*. The Supreme Court over­turned the ban on *Crossroads*, and the sedi­tion law, 124A, was struck down. {088-S04}

Nehru’s an­swer was the First Amendment, adding caveats such as pub­lic order and re­la­tions with friendly coun­tries. If the courts came in the way of the leg­is­la­ture on basic so­cial mat­ters, he ar­gued, it was for the leg­is­la­ture to amend the Constitution. {#nehru}

Opposition came even from peo­ple he re­spected: Acharya Kripalani, Jayaprakash Narayan and Syama Prasad Mookerjee. Naziruddin Ahmad, an MP from Bengal, warned that sedi­tion would come back. It did, on the grounds the amend­ment laid.
~ Amit Varma ad­mits he once wrongly said the amend­ment it­self re­vived sedi­tion, and was cor­rected. In spirit, he main­tains, it was true.
stories.why: Even a cel­e­brated lib­eral, sure that peo­ple like him will use power wisely, builds tools his ri­vals later in­herit. Today, Varma said, the boot is on the other foot, and every party in power uses these laws.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Nehru and the First Amendment

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a law against outraging religious feelings
stories.head: Beef, a wedding and a joke book
body: Section 295A pun­ishes de­lib­er­ate and ma­li­cious acts in­tended to out­rage re­li­gious feel­ings. Around 2007, Amit Varma wrote a col­umn on how it was being used. {088-S03}

Ravi Shastri, dur­ing cricket com­men­tary in a se­ries in South Africa, said he likes eat­ing beef. {#shastri} A 295A case was filed. Elizabeth Hurley mar­ried Arun Nayar with­out, ap­par­ently, all the Hindu rit­u­als. Another case. The pub­lisher of a Santa-Banta joke book got one too.
The law can be read any way you like, Varma said, and a case can be filed any­where. If it is filed in Tripura, you have to go to the court there.
~ Its cousins are no bet­ter. Section 153A cov­ers acts prej­u­di­cial to har­mony be­tween re­li­gious, racial, lan­guage or re­gional groups, and under it, Varma said, any­thing can be made to fit.
stories.why: Vague speech laws do their dam­age through the process it­self, what­ever the ver­dict. Anyone can be dragged across the coun­try over a re­mark about beef, a wed­ding or a joke, which is why Varma calls the process a pun­ish­ment.

stories.kicker: Roshan Abbas’s party story, as Amit Varma retold it
stories.head: Priyanka flopped, the baba boomed
body: At a party at Ajay Shah’s house, their friend Roshan Abbas told the hosts a story about Ranveer Allahbadia. One week the pod­caster re­leased an in­ter­view with Priyanka Chopra that he thought would go madly viral. Nothing hap­pened.
Then he put out an episode with an Aghori Baba. It got two mil­lion views in six hours, or there­abouts, and he em­braced tantra and Aghori con­tent. {088-S01}

Before the elec­tions, gov­ern­ment min­is­ters in­clud­ing Jaishankar and Piyush Goyal skipped the smaller right-wing pod­casts and went on his show. “Modiji com­pletely ig­nored those guys, just went for the num­bers,” Amit Varma said. {088-J04}
~ The left promptly branded Allahbadia a right-winger. He was no kind of winger, Varma said: just a cu­ri­ous host whose big guests asked to come on.
stories.why: Creators and politi­cians alike fol­low the num­bers. Labels are often pinned on a host for who ap­pears on the show, not for any­thing he be­lieves: that is how a pod­caster with no ide­ol­ogy be­came a tar­get for both sides.

quiz.a: Because the state is weak: fil­ing a case and going through courts is it­self pun­ish­ment.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 88. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: John Locke (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); Salman Rushdie (Elena Ternovaja, CC BY-SA 3.0); B. R. Ambedkar (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Matt Ridley (Chris McAndrew, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Sixteen Stormy Days
shelf.creator: Tripurdaman Singh
shelf.why: The de­fin­i­tive ac­count of India’s First Amendment, which, un­like America’s, was a blow against free speech: the Lok Sabha de­bates show Nehru tak­ing il­lib­eral po­si­tions to si­lence his ri­vals, a great states­man un­done by hubris.

shelf.title: The First Assault on Our Constitution (Episode 194 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Tripurdaman Singh
shelf.why: Tripurdaman Singh on the First Amendment to India’s Constitution, which Amit says badly harmed free speech in India: a con­ver­sa­tional way into the story Singh tells in Sixteen Stormy Days.

shelf.title: Nehru: The Debates that Defined India
shelf.creator: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
shelf.why: Nehru’s de­bates with Jinnah, Syama Prasad Mookerjee and Patel show fine minds dis­agree­ing in good faith over power and rights, a spirit of ‘as­sume goodwill’, lost in today’s dis­course, that Amit finds deeply in­spir­ing.

shelf.title: Nehru’s Debates (Episode 262 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma, Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain
shelf.why: Tripurdaman Singh and Adeel Hussain on the clashes that shaped India’s early con­sti­tu­tional pol­i­tics: a ‘sleeper hit’ that shows Nehru and Patel re­spect­ing each other while dis­agree­ing, against both car­i­ca­tures of their re­la­tion­ship.

shelf.title: Caged Tiger: How Too Much Government Is Holding Indians Back
shelf.creator: Subhashish Bhadra
shelf.why: Bhadra’s frame that con­sti­tu­tions are prod­ucts of their cir­cum­stances: America’s was built to pro­tect peo­ple from the state, while India’s, drafted amid tur­moil and frag­men­ta­tion, cen­tralised power to pro­tect the state from the peo­ple and paid only lip ser­vice to free­dom.

shelf.title: Subhashish Bhadra on Our Dysfunctional State (Episode 333 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Subhashish Bhadra
shelf.why: Subhashish Bhadra on India’s over­reach­ing state, built to rule rather than to serve: the longer con­ver­sa­tion be­hind his book Caged Tiger.

shelf.title: Shruti Rajagopalan’s 2015 talk on constitutional amendments over the decades
shelf.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
shelf.why: Shruti Rajagopalan’s talk trac­ing how India’s Constitution has been amended from Nehru on­wards when­ever gov­ern­ments wanted to do some­thing un­con­sti­tu­tional, until amend­ment be­came the rou­tine way to make the un­con­sti­tu­tional con­sti­tu­tional.

shelf.title: When Ideas Have Sex
shelf.creator: Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Ridley’s talk on why ideas must col­lide and re­com­bine freely for the best ones to emerge and for so­ci­ety to progress; the hosts apply it to con­tract­ing re­search out to uni­ver­si­ties and firms.

shelf.title: The First Amendment to the US Constitution
shelf.why: ‘Congress shall make no law... abridg­ing the free­dom of speech’ has no caveats.

shelf.title: Don’t Insult Pasta (2007)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A play­ful satire on de­mands not to of­fend re­li­gious sen­ti­ment (if you don’t want me to of­fend your god, don’t of­fend mine), part of Amit’s two decades of col­umns on free speech in India.

shelf.title: Fighting Against Censorship (2007)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Background read­ing on the Indian cen­sor­ship regime the episode cri­tiques.

shelf.title: Fascism in Baroda (2007)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Part of the ar­chive of real Indian free-speech bat­tles be­hind this episode’s ar­gu­ments.

shelf.title: Punish Rioters, Not Writers (2007)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The title sums up the prin­ci­ple Amit ar­gues in the episode: pun­ish the vi­o­lent act, not the words.

shelf.title: In Defence of Tanmay Bhat (2016)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A pre­cur­sor to his de­fence of Ranveer: stand­ing up for the speech rights of cre­ators under fire.

laughs.text: The car­toon Amit re­calls from the early Republic: some­one at the par­lia­ment book­store asks for a copy of the Constitution, and the clerk replies, ‘I’m afraid we don’t stock pe­ri­od­i­cals.’
Amit on hurt feel­ings: ‘We are adults. It’s not like we are kinder­garten chil­dren or Oh teacher, teacher, Ajay hurt my feel­ings, take away his tif­fin box.’

On the India’s Got Latent ed­i­tor being booked: ‘as young Nomsita would know, an editor’s job is to cut things out, and this ed­i­tor did not cut out the anap-shanap, as it were. Except that if you try to cut out ev­ery­thing that peo­ple will find ob­jec­tion­able from a com­edy show, you’ll ba­si­cally have noth­ing left.’ (Nomsita edits this show.)

Amit acts out Ranveer’s in­ter­view trick of re­peat­ing your last line back as a ques­tion: you say ‘free speech is im­por­tant for a democ­racy,’ and he goes, eyes wide, ‘Oh, free speech is im­por­tant for a democ­racy?’ Then you elab­o­rate for an­other two min­utes.

On ‘de­cency and morality’ as grounds for re­stric­tion: if Amit opened an­other cou­ple of shirt but­tons, ‘it of­fends de­cency and moral­ity. I mean, I might say it my­self, ac­tu­ally, frankly, be­cause I know what my chest looks like.’

Ajay’s test case for in­cite­ment: a tweet or­der­ing Amit’s 100,000 fol­low­ers to ‘get a glass of cold water and dunk it on Nomsita’s head.’ His fol­low­ers, being wise and sen­si­ble, know it’s hu­mour and no water lands on her head. Deciding such cases is what judges are for.
Hanlon’s razor (‘never at­tribute to mal­ice what can be ad­e­quately ex­plained by stupidity’), which Amit ap­plies to Ranveer as per­haps ig­no­rance: ‘I don’t want to call him stupid.’
Ambedkar’s early-1950s lament, as re­counted by Amit: he had been proud of the Constitution, but see­ing what was being done to it, ‘I would gladly burn it my­self.’
Wright’s Law, in Ajay’s rant about being forced to rebut so­cial-media ru­mours: a com­pany should be busy get­ting ‘twenty per­cent gains for each dou­bling of output’, not polic­ing chat groups.
